transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Lydia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Sara Velasquez (NimbleCore Head of ML), Tom Rivera (NimbleCore Infra), Mohammed Ali (NimbleCore Security)

Summary (auto):
NimbleCore is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for production inference of a mixed workload (real-time chat + batch rerank). Primary concerns: tenant isolation, eviction tolerance and warm-pool burst behavior, KMS integration and audit logs, and clear cost/commitment tradeoffs. They requested a synthetic spike test and SOC2 + encryption docs.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and traffic profile
- Isolation and eviction scenarios (preemption, warm pools)
- Burst strategy (hot pool, prewarm, throttles, queueing)
- Compliance (KMS, audit logs, SSO)
- Pricing/commitment tiers and SLAs

Transcript:
[00:00] Lydia (Redwood): hi everyone thanks for joining, let's do quick intros and then walk through what you need from dedicated capacity
[00:06] Sara (NimbleCore): hey thanks, sara here. we're running a mix of low-latency chat for our product and nightly reranks, looking to move off our self-hosted k8s cluster for production inference
[00:14] Tom (NimbleCore): hi tom, infra. mostly concerned about eviction during spikes and how isolation looks for multi-tenant workloads
[00:21] Mohammed (NimbleCore): and security questions, kms, audit logs, SOC2 — that's big for us
[00:28] Marcus (Redwood): great, i'll sketch the technical picture; lydia will handle commercials. to start—can you share p50/p95 latencies and your peak qps?
[00:36] Sara: p50 around 90ms for small-chat-ish prompts, p95 ~380ms, peak qps ~600 for chat, but we have daily spikes up to 1.8k for a few minutes after our lunchtime release window, and nightly batch jobs that need throughput but can be queued
[00:50] Tom: important detail — some of our traffic is long-context doc summarization, seq len ~2k tokens, KV cache is important, can't really afford repeated cold KV recompute on eviction
[00:59] Lydia: understood. on Redwood Dedicated we offer reserved pools with optional warm/hot pool pre-warm. when a reserved node is evicted we can fall back to a lower-cost hosted variant or to a warm pool — depends on your SLOs
[01:12] Sara: we tried another provider where warm pools were slow to kick in, like 30-90s which was catastrophic for user-facing flows
[01:19] Marcus: right, that cold-start delta is what we optimize for: we do prefix KV caching, and for reserved pools we can maintain sticky hot pools per tenant that keep cache resident; for longer sequences we recommend keeping a small fraction of GPUs warm for your highest-traffic tenants
[01:33] Mohammed: how does encryption work if we want KMS in our own account? we need envelope encryption and HSM-backed keys ideally
[01:40] Lydia: we support customer-managed keys via KMS integrations in Dedicated and Private—envelope keys, and audit logs accessible via our console and optional syslog/S3 delivery
[01:49] Tom: about eviction—what are the policies? does Redwood evict reserved nodes for higher-priority jobs? what's the worst-case for us?
[01:57] Marcus: reserved capacity means we aim to guarantee compute for you; eviction generally only occurs during failover scenarios or maintenance. for reserved pool preemption we have defined eviction windows and we provide graceful drain hooks and configurable fallback policies — e.g., route to hosted equivalent, fall back to a quantized model, or queue requests briefly. We can model worst-case based on commitment tier — higher commitments reduce eviction probability
[02:18] Sara: can you quantify — like 0.01% chance per month for x tier?
[02:22] Lydia: we can provide historical telemetry for similar accounts; we'll include probabilistic eviction models in the follow-up docs. Our SLO language ties back to burst allowances and warm-pool sizes
[02:33] Tom: we also need to understand tenant fencing — how isolated is the memory/KV cache? if two tenants share a GPU, is there leakage risk?
[02:41] Marcus: good question. Dedicated gives node-level tenancy; we do not co-locate across different customers on the same GPU for Dedicated. For Dedicated Reserved pools within the same customer, we can shard tenants into different instances; KV cache is per model/tenant instance and doesn't cross tenant boundaries. there are escape mitigations at runtime and hypervisor level as well
[03:02] Mohammed: and for Private on-prem — we'd prefer that for PHI, but it's heavier — how does the handoff look?
[03:08] Lydia: Private is an option for regulated workloads; typical path is start on Dedicated Hosted in Redwood region for functional validation then transition to Private or VPC-attached nodes. handoff includes config sync, key handover, and an on-prem agent for metrics and traces
[03:22] Sara: cost is a big factor — we have finance thresholds. what's the tradeoff between larger warm pools vs higher commit tiers?
[03:28] Marcus: warm pools are optimized to reduce tail latency at the cost of idle GPU time; committing larger reserved pools gets you lower unit price and lower eviction risk. There's a diminishing return curve: doubling warm pool usually reduces tail bleed but at linear cost increase; we'll show sample models in the pricing sheet
[03:43] Tom: curious about burst shaping — if we get sudden 3x spike, does Redwood queue or throttle? we want graceful degradation not 503s
[03:50] Marcus: we recommend layered approach: (1) request-level rate limits + token-based throttles, (2) short queuing windows with adaptive timeouts, and (3) fallback to a smaller quantized model for very high load. We can also front-load traffic across regions if you allow multi-region routing
[04:06] Sara: we use a few very large instruction-tuned models, ~30B quantized to int8 for cost reasons — will that affect your warm pool behavior?
[04:13] Marcus: int8 quantization reduces memory footprint so warm pool is cheaper; however your cache behavior still depends on kv size for long contexts. we can recommend a mix: dedicate 1-2 nodes for heavy-long-context traffic and keep several fast nodes for short chat flows
[04:27] Mohammed: auditability — we need immutable logs for inference inputs for a subset of users, retention 2 years, and SSO integration for RBAC. is that supported?
[04:35] Lydia: yes; audit logs can be exported, tamper-evident delivery options exist, and we integrate with SAML SSO for RBAC. retention is configurable; longer retention is part of an enterprise add-on
[04:46] Tom: any known limits on concurrency per GPU? like 8 concurrent chats vs 1 heavy summarization?
[04:51] Marcus: concurrency depends on model size and latencies; for a 30B int8 model we typically aim for 6-12 concurrent low-latency streams per A100-equivalent; single large-sequence jobs will be scheduled with affinity. We'll run a profiling pass with your traces
[05:06] Sara: about the spike test — we'd like a 24-hour synthetic run that includes 5x sustained spikes for 10 minutes every 2 hours, and a few 30-minute stress windows. can you do that in a Dedicated sandbox?
[05:16] Marcus: yes, we can spin up an isolated slice in Dedicated sandbox, run the test, capture latencies, eviction occurrences, and cache miss rates. that's exactly what we'll propose in the test plan
[05:27] Lydia: commercially — rough pricing tiers: monthly reserved vCPU/GPU commits with warm-pool addon and hotpool per-tenant; i'll send the detailed sheet. we can do a pilot at discounted rates if you commit to a 6-month trial
[05:40] Sara: finance will push back on any long idle costs; we need to show ROI — are there batching/caching savings numbers you can share?
[05:47] Marcus: yes — for workloads with repeating prefixes our prefix cache can reduce token compute by 25-60% depending on locality. we'll include a sample calc using your submitted traces
[05:58] Tom: operationally— we need runbooks for failover, and playbooks for rollback if model quality regresses after quantization. do you support automatic canary rollouts?
[06:06] Lydia: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B, automatic fallback to previous model if metrics degrade, and slow rollouts by percentage. We'll share runbook templates
[06:18] Mohammed: legal — do you support data residency in eu-west region and do you hold any customer data in plaintext?
[06:25] Lydia: we offer regional deployments and data residency controls; payloads are encrypted in transit and at rest. for Dedicated we don't store payloads unless configured for logging; and for compliance we can provide encryption proofs
[06:36] Sara: okay next steps?
[06:38] Lydia: action items — i'll send pricing and SOC2/KMS papers; Marcus will send the spike test plan; Tom to share traffic histograms; we'll do the 1-day spike test and reconvene. recommended timeline — docs and pricing in 2-3 business days and run the test next week if you can sign the pilot
[06:52] Tom: i'll get histograms to you by friday
[06:55] Mohammed: can you include a sample SLA clause for eviction tolerance? we'll need to review legal before committing
[06:59] Lydia: yes, sample SLA clause will be attached to the pricing email
[07:03] Sara: thank you. one last thing — competitor comparison: we tried Lambda Labs and had preemption issues; we want something that behaves predictably under load
[07:11] Lydia: understood — we'll include comparative notes and telemetry where possible
[07:14] End of call
